title: NAB backs down on Christmas redundancies
full_text:
National Australia Bank has backed down on its plan to make more than 1500 staff redundant before Christmas, agreeing to give workers on the chopping block a reprieve following intense public and political backlash.
The big four banks will now keep staff who are made involuntarily redundant until January 27, five weeks later than planned. The new date also applies to workers who cannot find different roles at the bank.
The extension comes after NAB was widely criticised for cutting 1500 staff so close to the end of the year, and Labor MPs also took aim at the role of artificial intelligence and offshoring in the decision.
"Since the start of consultation on 22 October, many of you have shared thoughtful feedback on the impact on teams, how work will be done under the proposed future operating model and what this means for affected colleagues," chief executive Andrew Irvine told staff in an email.
"You have raised concerns about the proximity to Christmas, expressing a desire for more time to consider deployment options. We have listened."
Those who opt out of redeployment will leave the bank on December 16, two weeks later than scheduled, and those who take a voluntary payout will depart on December 2 as planned.
With scheduled pay rises at the bank coming into effect on January 1, many staff will now receive bigger payouts.
NAB will report its full-year results on Thursday and is expected to announce a $6.35 billion cash profit. Analysts estimate the restructuring will save between $400 million and $450 million a year.
The bank has also granted one more week of consultation with staff to allow affected employees more time to lodge an expression of interest in a new role.
The Finance Sector Union had threatened to take NAB to the Fair Work Commission over its handling of the restructuring, which it said was among the worst it had witnessed.
Irvine met union representatives twice last week as the bank tried to avoid further escalation before he and the other big four chief executives are questioned by a parliamentary committee next week.
He described the engagement as constructive, and pointed staff towards support services offered by the organisation. The union said the extension would give workers and their families more certainty over the Christmas period and facilitate "genuine consultation".
Staff had said they were given little clarity about their futures at the bank, describing communication from management as inconsistent and complaining that the restructuring lacked detail.
Many are now locked into a Hunger Games-esque "spill and fill" process in which more than 3200 of them must compete with their own colleagues for half as many jobs.
After the reprieve over the new year, 1500 staff will be pushed into a job market replete with rivals from other big banks and financial services companies that are all trimming headcounts.
